title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Autism — October 2026

studies.title: Autistic children feel others' distress more strongly — but read it less accurately
studies.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: a direct challenge to the "autistic people lack empathy" trope, backed by behavioral, physiological and eye-tracking data in a decent-sized sample; limited by a modest control group and single site.
studies.the_study: Researchers at UCLA showed five videos of children displaying strong sadness or anger to 103 autistic and 40 non-autistic children aged 6–13, matched demographically, while recording skin conductance and eye gaze and coding their spoken reactions for emotional contagion and perspective taking. Autistic children reacted with *greater* affective and physiological intensity than non-autistic children, yet identified the on-screen emotions less accurately. The proposed mechanism: intense arousal drove attention shifting away from the face, which degraded emotion recognition, which in turn predicted less emotional synchrony, less perspective taking and lower prosocial motivation.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes a core stereotype — the apparent flatness some autistic children show toward others' distress may be downstream of feeling too much, not too little, and of looking away to cope.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a child who bursts into tears at a classmate's upset and then turns their back — behavior routinely read as indifference. The finding to lead on: autistic children's sweat-gland responses and self-reported feelings were *stronger* than their peers', while their emotion labeling was worse, and the two were causally linked in the model via gaze shifting. Call Jeffrey J. Wood at UCLA, who proposes the Emotion Regulation and Recognition Account, and Sondre Orm in Norway for the measurement side. Note this is a case-control design testing a new model, not a treatment trial.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on how "empathy" became the single most misused word in autism science — from Baron-Cohen's early theories through the double empathy problem to intense-world theory — and what happens to autistic adults when clinicians, courts and employers interpret overwhelm as coldness. Fits a long-read in a general-interest magazine or a psychology title.
studies.caveats: Non-autistic comparison group is small (n=40); observational case-control design cannot establish the causal pathway the model proposes; laboratory videos may not reflect real-world social encounters; the model is explicitly described as preliminary.

studies.title: A cord blood enzyme at birth tracks autism traits six years later — in the opposite direction to expectations
studies.ns_score_reason: a large prospective birth cohort with a clinician-observed outcome at age 6 and a result that runs against the prevailing neuroinflammation narrative; purely observational and needs replication.
studies.the_study: In the Hamamatsu Birth Cohort for Mothers and Children, researchers measured soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) — an enzyme that breaks down anti-inflammatory lipid mediators — in umbilical cord serum from 854 newborns, then assessed autism symptom severity at age 6 using the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule. Higher sEH at birth was associated with *lower* symptom severity after adjustment for confounders, with effects on both social affect and restricted/repetitive behavior scores apparent in boys but not girls. sEH also correlated negatively with the inflammatory marker MCP-1, though MCP-1 itself showed no relationship with ADOS scores.
studies.why_it_matters: sEH inhibitors are in development as anti-inflammatory psychiatric drugs on the assumption that less sEH activity is better for the brain; this cohort points the other way for early neurodevelopment, and suggests the lipid-signaling story is more sex-specific and less straightforward than assumed.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the inversion — an enzyme that researchers have spent a decade trying to block turns out to be associated with *fewer* autism traits when it is abundant at birth, and only in boys. Open on the practice of banking cord blood in birth cohorts and what those freezers are now yielding. Worth calling Hideo Matsuzaki at the University of Fukui and Bruce Hammock at UC Davis, whose lab pioneered sEH inhibitors, for a candid read on what this does to the hypothesis. Frame strictly as association — this is not a predictive test and nothing follows for expectant parents.
studies.wider_angle: A reported piece on the sex gap in autism biomarker research: why so many prenatal signals appear in boys and vanish in girls, and whether that reflects biology, diagnostic instruments calibrated on male presentations, or both. Good fit for a specialist health or women's-health outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish causation; single Japanese cohort, may not generalize; outcome is dimensional symptom severity in a general-population sample rather than diagnosed autism; the proposed MCP-1 mechanism was not supported; multiple subgroup comparisons.

studies.title: Autism is over-represented in binge eating too — not just anorexia
studies.ns_score_reason: genuinely corrects a lopsided literature and a clinical blind spot, and readers with eating disorders will recognize themselves; held back by being a narrative review of methodologically thin studies.
studies.the_study: Researchers at King's College London and the Maudsley reviewed the emerging evidence on autism in bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder — conditions largely ignored by a field that has concentrated almost entirely on anorexia. They report that autism appears over-represented in binge-type eating disorders, though at lower rates than in anorexia, and that reward processing, emotional regulation and sensory differences may drive binge presentations. Co-occurring ADHD emerges as a complicating factor in both recognition and treatment.
studies.why_it_matters: Eating disorder services that have begun adapting for autistic patients have built those adaptations almost entirely on an anorexia template — meaning autistic people who binge may be getting adjustments designed for a different problem, or none at all.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the asymmetry: the autism–anorexia link has been covered extensively, while an autistic person with binge eating disorder is likely to go unrecognized entirely. Open on sensory overload and interoception — the difficulty some autistic people have reading hunger and fullness signals — as a route into binge eating that nobody screens for. Call Kate Tchanturia and Lauren Makin at King's, who run one of the few autism-adapted eating disorder services in the world. Be clear this is a review flagging a research gap, not new prevalence data.
studies.wider_angle: A service-delivery investigation for a health-policy or clinical outlet: how many eating disorder services screen for autism at all, what the adaptations actually consist of, and whether the growing "neurodivergence-informed care" movement has evidence behind it or is running ahead of the data.
studies.caveats: Narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis; the authors themselves describe the underlying prevalence research as methodologically limited; no new primary data; the autistic samples in reviewed studies are likely skewed toward diagnosed, help-seeking individuals.

studies.title: Brain scans suggest autism comes in two structural flavors
studies.ns_score_reason: a credible attempt to carve up autism's notorious neuroimaging heterogeneity with a disease-progression algorithm, but it is a secondary analysis of an open dataset with only weak clinical correlates.
studies.the_study: Researchers applied Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) — an algorithm developed for tracking neurodegenerative disease progression — to structural MRI scans in the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE I and II). Two gray-matter patterns emerged consistently: one centered on cerebellar, limbic and striatal regions, the other on anterior fronto-cingulo-insular regions. In exploratory analyses, progression along the first was linked to lower verbal IQ and the second to modestly higher ADOS scores, and the subtypes could be separated by machine learning across independent cohorts within ABIDE.
studies.why_it_matters: Decades of autism brain imaging have produced contradictory findings — more gray matter here, less there — and this offers a concrete explanation: group averages may be blending two different anatomical patterns that cancel each other out. It is a framework for future work rather than anything usable in a clinic.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the long-running embarrassment of autism neuroimaging — thousands of scans, no replicable brain signature — and the possibility that researchers have been averaging apples and oranges. The hook is the borrowed tool: an algorithm built to stage Alzheimer's disease repurposed to sort a developmental condition. Call Cheng Luo at the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, and an independent ABIDE veteran for a reality check on whether two subtypes survive outside this dataset. Avoid any suggestion that scans can diagnose or subtype an individual.
studies.wider_angle: A critical piece for a science or data-focused outlet on the proliferation of subtyping algorithms across psychiatry — autism, depression "biotypes", schizophrenia clusters — and the uncomfortable track record of such clusters failing to replicate in fresh samples.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of a pooled, retrospective, multi-site open dataset; clinical associations described by the authors as exploratory and modest; cross-cohort validation was within ABIDE rather than fully independent; no longitudinal scanning despite the "stage" framing; ABIDE skews male and high-IQ, so results may not generalize.

studies.title: Prenatal supplements for preventing autism and ADHD: the evidence isn't there
studies.ns_score_reason: a clear, usable corrective to a booming supplement market and a lot of overexcited headlines, but it is a narrative review with no new data.
studies.the_study: Reviewers organized the human evidence on prenatal dietary patterns, choline and polyphenols by how directly each study measured outcomes — diagnosed autism or ADHD, dimensional traits, or general neurodevelopment. Whole-diet studies offered the strongest human evidence but produced cohort-dependent results vulnerable to familial and genetic confounding. Choline trials addressed attention and general cognition, not diagnosed conditions; polyphenol evidence rested on food proxies and a single trimester-specific cohort. The authors conclude the field is "an organizing framework rather than a confirmed causal hypothesis" and explicitly advise against high-dose single-nutrient or concentrated-polyphenol supplementation.
studies.why_it_matters: Prenatal choline and polyphenol supplements are marketed on the back of rodent studies and cognitive-trait findings; this review draws a firm line between those and any claim about preventing autism or ADHD.
studies.pitch_angle: Open in the supplement aisle, or on a pregnancy forum thread about choline dosing, then work backward to what the human trials actually measured — and did not. The surprise for readers is how much of the enthusiasm traces to specific mouse strains (BTBR, Ts65Dn) and valproate-exposed rats. Call Simone Perna at the University of Milan. The responsible framing is the authors' own: aim for dietary adequacy, not megadoses.
studies.wider_angle: An investigation for a consumer-health or business outlet into how prenatal supplement marketing claims are regulated in the US, UK and EU, and how far preclinical rodent data can legally travel into a product label.
studies.caveats: Narrative review with a purposive rather than systematic search; no new primary data; underlying cohort studies are observational and prone to residual confounding; much of the supporting mechanism is animal work.

studies.title: An eight-week parent-led program keeps autistic teenagers' job skills from sliding over the summer
studies.ns_score_reason: a randomized two-group design addressing a real and under-studied gap, and one of very few autism intervention trials from the Gulf; undercut by small N, parent-reported outcomes and retrospective registration.
studies.the_study: Sixty-four Saudi parent–child dyads, with autistic adolescents and young adults aged 15–21, were randomly allocated to an eight-week digital program (SAVOR) or a waitlist. Parents worked through eight short asynchronous modules and ran structured vocational readiness activities at home. Retention was 90.6%, nearly 90% of intervention parents completed all modules, and parent-reported vocational readiness favored the program (adjusted mean difference 6.1, Cohen's d = 0.58), with the largest gains in self-management and time management. Five autistic participants also gave direct feedback, describing a sense of accomplishment and independence alongside difficulty starting tasks.
studies.why_it_matters: The long summer break is a well-known regression risk for autistic young people yet almost no research targets it; this is an early signal that a low-intensity, parent-delivered program might hold the line — but the authors are explicit that it does not establish effectiveness.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the overlooked eight weeks of the year — what happens to transition-age autistic young people when school structure disappears, and whether parents can plausibly fill the gap with 15 minutes a day. Open on a family's summer timetable. Call Abdulrahman F. Aldakhil at Majmaah University. Be straight with readers that this is a feasibility pilot with parent-rated outcomes, and that the researchers themselves are calling for a properly powered, pre-registered trial.
studies.wider_angle: A piece for an education or international-development outlet on the rapid build-out of autism transition services in Saudi Arabia under Vision 2030, and the broader question of whether interventions designed in North America and Europe can be culturally adapted or need building from scratch.
studies.caveats: Small N (64 dyads); outcomes almost entirely parent-reported, with only five autistic participants giving direct feedback; waitlist control means no blinding and no placebo comparison; not prospectively registered (retrospectively registered on OSF); no follow-up beyond post-intervention; single-country sample.

studies.title: Caregivers of children with congenital CMV report *less* emotional strain when autism is in the picture — at school age
studies.journal: Journal of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely odd age-dependent reversal that invites an adaptation hypothesis, but the recruitment method and sample size make it more of a prompt than a finding.
studies.the_study: Caregivers of 181 children with congenital cytomegalovirus, recruited via social media and nonprofit channels, completed quality-of-life questionnaires, split into toddlers (1 to under 4) and school-age children (4 to under 11). Severity markers at birth dropped out of the models once current conditions were accounted for: what predicted family impact was how the child functions now. Among toddlers, autism and seizures were linked to more negative caregiver emotional impact — but among school-age children, autism and seizure disorder were both associated with *less* negative emotional impact. Family cohesion was unrelated to clinical characteristics at either age.
studies.why_it_matters: It hints that the distress associated with a child's diagnosis is heavily front-loaded around the period of uncertainty and diagnosis, and may ease as families adapt — a pattern clinicians describe anecdotally but rarely capture in data.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the reversal and the question it raises: does the emotional weight of a diagnosis peak early and then fall as families build competence and find services? Open on a parent in the diagnostic limbo of the toddler years. Call Megan Pesch at the University of Michigan, who works on both cCMV and developmental-behavioral pediatrics. Flag plainly that this is a cross-sectional comparison of two age bands, not the same families followed over time, and that self-selected online recruitment could easily produce this pattern.
studies.wider_angle: A public-health feature on congenital CMV itself — the most common infectious cause of birth defects, barely known to the public, with no routine screening in most countries and a simple set of pregnancy hygiene precautions that almost nobody is told about. Fits a general-interest or parenting-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational and cross-sectional — the age pattern is between groups, not within families over time; convenience sample recruited through social media and advocacy organizations, likely skewed toward engaged, resourced and more severely affected families; all outcomes caregiver-reported; N=181 split across two age strata, so subgroup estimates are imprecise; autism status is parent-reported rather than independently confirmed.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- The "autistic people lack empathy" story continues to come apart from two directions. Last month's *Autism Research* finding that empathy amplifies rather than buffers the emotional cost of social withdrawal (PMID 42670580) now sits alongside "Autistic children feel others' distress more strongly — but read it less accurately" (PMID 42856069), which supplies a physiological mechanism: stronger skin-conductance and self-reported responses, worse emotion labeling, gaze shifting in between. Both point the same way — not absent feeling, but feeling that costs something.
- That also extends the "effort behind matched or apparently poorer performance" thread from the pupillometry study of visual perspective-taking (PMID 41992731). In the new UCLA work the overwhelm is measured in sweat glands rather than pupils, but the structure of the claim is identical: what is scored as a social deficit is partly a regulation problem.

**Advances**
- Interoception and eating were flagged last month as a side note to the body-image work in autistic adults (PMID 42566953). "Autism is over-represented in binge eating too" (PMID 42850402) turns that into a clinical agenda, moving the autism–eating disorder conversation off its anorexia-only track.
- The warning about pooled-sample neuroimaging raised by the diffusion MRI group-by-brain reversal (PMID 42619183) gets a proposed fix rather than a rebuttal: "Brain scans suggest autism comes in two structural flavors" (PMID 42853485) applies a neurodegeneration staging algorithm to ABIDE precisely on the argument that group averages have been blending incompatible anatomies. The two studies make a natural pair — one diagnosing the problem, one attempting a remedy, both on samples too small or too retrospective to settle it.
- Parent-as-delivery-mechanism research moves from preschool emotion regulation (PMID 42665438) and online parent-child interaction therapy (PMID 42660578) to transition age: the Saudi SAVOR trial of an eight-week parent-led vocational program (PMID 42790248). Same logic, much older children, and the first of these to target employment rather than behavior.

**Counterpoints**
- Last month's genomic structural equation modeling questioned "the biological basis for disproportionate prevalence rates in males" (PMID 42658390). The cord blood enzyme cohort (PMID 42843280) cuts the other way, reporting a prenatal biological signal for symptom severity in boys and not girls. Common-variant genetics and prenatal lipid signaling are not the same level of analysis, but a journalist writing about autism's sex gap now has two fresh papers pulling in opposite directions — worth putting to both groups.

**New themes**
- Prenatal and perinatal biology is new to this run: the cord blood sEH cohort (PMID 42843280) and the review finding the evidence for prenatal choline, polyphenol and dietary prevention of autism and ADHD "isn't there" (PMID 42849536). The September batch was almost entirely behavioral, genetic and service-focused.
- Caregiver trajectory over time, rather than caregiver burden as a fixed quantity: the congenital CMV study's age-dependent reversal (PMID 42853118) is a different question from the sibling-expectations work last month (PMID 42537268), though both concern how families plan around a diagnosis.
- Geographic broadening continues, with Saudi Arabia (PMID 42790248) joining last month's Hong Kong, Brazil/Spain and UAE studies — and, as before, these are the studies with the smallest samples and weakest designs.

---
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies in this batch each show a clinical or service template built around the wrong autistic patient. Eating disorder services have adapted for autism almost entirely on an anorexia model, while autistic people who binge go unrecognized (PMID 42850402); autistic children's intense physiological distress is scored as indifference because they look away (PMID 42856069); caregiver emotional strain, assumed to accumulate, is lower at school age than in toddlerhood (PMID 42853118); and the eight weeks of summer, when transition-age support simply stops, has almost no intervention research behind it (PMID 42790248).

**Why pitch this now:** Services across the UK, US and Gulf are busy branding themselves "neurodivergence-informed" and adapting existing pathways for autistic patients — and this cluster suggests several of those adaptations are being generalized from a narrow prototype, usually a school-age boy with the best-studied presentation.

**Angle:** A reported feature following autistic people through the services that were supposedly adjusted for them — an eating disorder clinic, a school transition program, a diagnostic assessment — asking who the adaptation was actually designed around and what happens to everyone else. Written for clinicians, commissioners and autistic adults and their families, concrete about costs and waiting lists rather than abstract about neurodiversity.

**Potential headlines:**
- Autism-adapted clinics are being built around one kind of autistic patient
- The children who looked indifferent had the strongest stress responses
- Your autism adjustments were designed for someone with a different profile

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — Mind territory, but the argument needs several services and three or four studies to land, which rules out a news slot.
- **STAT** — strongest on the clinical-service version: how eating disorder and transition programs decide what an "autism adaptation" consists of, and on what evidence.
- **The Transmitter** — the autism research readership is precisely where the prototype problem (who the instruments and services were calibrated on) gets argued out.
- **The Guardian** science and health desk — King's/Maudsley is a UK anchor, and the paper has run sustained coverage of autism assessment and eating disorder service failures.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Autism — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-12 | **Studies reviewed:** 7
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind autism digest (run 2026-10-12)

---

### Study 1: Autistic children feel others' distress more strongly — but read it less accurately
**PMID:** 42856069 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (two Moderate)

**Issue A. Group difference in physiological reactivity not reported** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Autistic children reacted with *greater* affective and physiological intensity than non-autistic children, yet identified the on-screen emotions less accurately."
- **Abstract says:** "Autistic children experienced greater affective intensity but exhibited less accurate emotion recognition than non-autistic children when observing youth exhibiting strong affect. Greater physiological and affective intensity were associated with greater attention shifting…"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a *between-group* difference only for affective intensity. Physiological (electrodermal) intensity appears only as a within-sample predictor of attention shifting — there is no stated finding that autistic children were physiologically more reactive than controls. The pitch angle repeats the error more vividly: "autistic children's sweat-gland responses and self-reported feelings were *stronger* than their peers'."
- **Suggested fix:** "Autistic children reported *greater* affective intensity than non-autistic children, yet identified the on-screen emotions less accurately; across the sample, greater affective and physiological intensity went with more attention shifting." And in the pitch angle: "autistic children's self-reported emotional reactions were *stronger* than their peers', while their emotion labelling was worse."

**Issue B. Causal language for a case-control model** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the two were causally linked in the model via gaze shifting"
- **Abstract says:** "…more frequent attention shifting among autistic children was associated with less accurate emotion recognition" and, in the conclusions, "These reactions *may* lead to attention shifting."
- **Problem:** Every link in the chain is reported as an association in a cross-sectional case-control design. The caveats correctly say the design "cannot establish the causal pathway the model proposes," but the pitch body text asserts the opposite, which is the version a commissioning editor will read first.
- **Suggested fix:** "and the two were linked in the model via gaze shifting — an association, not a demonstrated causal chain."

**Issue C. "Away from the face" is an addition** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "intense arousal drove attention shifting away from the face, which degraded emotion recognition"
- **Abstract says:** "Electrodermal reactivity to and eye gaze towards the videos were also measured… greater attention shifting."
- **Problem:** The abstract refers to gaze toward the videos and "attention shifting" generically; it does not specify shifting away from faces. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "intense arousal was associated with more attention shifting away from the videos…"

**Issue D. Novelty label and NS fit score** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research" / "**NS fit:** 8/10"
- **Abstract says:** "Recent evidence suggests that many autistic individuals exhibit heightened emotional responsiveness to others' affect despite greater difficulty recognizing others' emotions… This study introduces and preliminarily evaluates the Emotion Regulation and Recognition Account (ERRA)."
- **Problem:** The paper builds on an existing line of recent evidence and offers "initial support" for a new model; it overturns a popular stereotype, not prior research. 8/10 is defensible on sample and multimodal measurement, but sits a notch high for an explicitly preliminary model evaluation.
- **Suggested fix:** Novelty: "Challenges a popular assumption"; NS fit 7/10.

---

### Study 2: A cord blood enzyme at birth tracks autism traits six years later
**PMID:** 42843280 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (one Moderate)

**Issue A. Suggested "independent" commentator is a co-author** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Worth calling Hideo Matsuzaki at the University of Fukui and Bruce Hammock at UC Davis, whose lab pioneered sEH inhibitors, for a candid read on what this does to the hypothesis."
- **Abstract says:** Author list includes "Morisseau CH(5), Hammock BD(6)" — "Department of Entomology and Nematology, and UCD Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of California Davis."
- **Problem:** Hammock is an author on this very paper, so he cannot serve as the outside reality check the pitch implies. The framing would mislead a commissioning editor about the independence of the quote.
- **Suggested fix:** "Worth calling the corresponding authors Nagisa Hata and Hideo Matsuzaki at the University of Fukui, and co-author Bruce Hammock at UC Davis, whose lab pioneered sEH inhibitors — then an independent sEH researcher for a candid read on what this does to the hypothesis."

**Issue B. Enzyme description not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) — an enzyme that breaks down anti-inflammatory lipid mediators"
- **Abstract says:** "Soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) is involved in regulating neuroinflammation implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) pathophysiology."
- **Problem:** The mechanistic gloss is standard biochemistry but is not stated in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only; keep it attributed to background rather than to this paper.
- **Suggested fix:** "soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) — an enzyme the authors describe as a regulator of neuroinflammation (and which degrades anti-inflammatory epoxy fatty acids)"

*Everything else checks out:* N = 854, cord serum ELISA, ADOS at 6 years, overall inverse association with calibrated severity scores, boy-specific effects on social affect, restricted/repetitive behaviour and CSS, null in girls, negative sEH–MCP-1 correlation, null MCP-1–ADOS link, and the explicit "causal relationships remain unclear" caveat. NS fit 7/10 is defensible for a prospective cohort of this size with a clinician-administered outcome.

---

### Study 3: Autism is over-represented in binge eating too — not just anorexia
**PMID:** 42850402 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Drive" overstates "may contribute"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "reward processing, emotional regulation and sensory differences may drive binge presentations"
- **Abstract says:** "Recent studies suggest that affective and reward-related processes, alongside sensory differences, may contribute to binge-type presentations."
- **Problem:** "Drive" implies a primary causal role; the review says "may contribute," and this is a narrative synthesis of methodologically limited studies.
- **Suggested fix:** "affective and reward-related processes, alongside sensory differences, may contribute to binge presentations"

**Issue B. Novelty label** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "This review summarises emerging evidence on Autism in binge-type EDs… Current AN-centric models may inadequately capture Neurodivergence in binge-type EDs."
- **Problem:** The review broadens an anorexia-focused literature and flags a gap; it does not overturn prior findings. "Corrects a field-wide blind spot" is the accurate label, and the digest's own caveat ("a review flagging a research gap, not new prevalence data") supports that.
- **Suggested fix:** Novelty: "Fills a documented evidence gap."

**Issue C. Unverified claims about the service and about screening** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Kate Tchanturia and Lauren Makin at King's, who run one of the few autism-adapted eating disorder services in the world" / "a route into binge eating that nobody screens for"
- **Abstract says:** "Autism also remains under-recognised in binge-type EDs by ED services, where existing adaptations remain largely derived from AN models."
- **Problem:** Both the "one of the few in the world" superlative and the interoception/screening claim are unverifiable from the abstract; "nobody screens for" overshoots "under-recognised."
- **Suggested fix:** "…who work on autism-adapted eating disorder care at the Maudsley (verify the service description before pitching)" and "a route into binge eating that services rarely screen for."

NS fit 6/10 is defensible for a narrative review with a clear clinical hook.

---

### Study 4: Brain scans suggest autism comes in two structural flavours
**PMID:** 42853485 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Clinical associations came from the sign-reversed model** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "In exploratory analyses, progression along the first was linked to lower verbal IQ and the second to modestly higher ADOS scores"
- **Abstract says:** "In exploratory covariate-adjusted analyses, higher stage in sign-reversed-model S1 was associated with lower verbal intelligence quotient (IQ) scores, whereas S2 showed modestly higher Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) scores."
- **Problem:** The association is specific to the sign-reversed z-score representation, not to the subtypes in general. A writer working from the digest would state it more broadly than the authors did.
- **Suggested fix:** "In exploratory analyses within the sign-reversed model, higher stage on the first subtype was linked to lower verbal IQ and the second showed modestly higher ADOS scores"

**Issue B. "Built to stage Alzheimer's disease"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "an algorithm built to stage Alzheimer's disease repurposed to sort a developmental condition"
- **Abstract says:** "We applied Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) to structural MRI data…" (no disease of origin specified; the digest body says "an algorithm developed for tracking neurodegenerative disease progression," which is also not in the abstract).
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — correct in the wider literature, but should be sourced elsewhere before it anchors the hook.
- **Suggested fix:** "an algorithm first developed for staging neurodegenerative disease (check SuStaIn's original application before leading on Alzheimer's)."

Headline "comes in two structural flavors" is adequately hedged by "suggest," and the caveats correctly note the within-ABIDE validation, exploratory clinical correlates, retrospective pooled dataset and absent longitudinal scanning. NS fit 5/10 is well judged.

---

### Study 5: Prenatal supplements for preventing autism and ADHD: the evidence isn't there
**PMID:** 42849536 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Explicitly advise against" is stronger than the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "explicitly advise against high-dose single-nutrient or concentrated-polyphenol supplementation"
- **Abstract says:** "Clinical translation should prioritize achieving recommended dietary adequacy and balanced dietary patterns; evidence does not support high-dose single-nutrient or concentrated-polyphenol supplementation for ASD/ADHD prevention."
- **Problem:** "Evidence does not support" is an absence-of-evidence statement; "advise against" converts it into a recommendation against use. In a consumer-health pitch that difference matters.
- **Suggested fix:** "and conclude that the evidence does not support high-dose single-nutrient or concentrated-polyphenol supplementation for ASD/ADHD prevention."

**Issue B. Quotation attached to the wrong subject** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The authors conclude the field is 'an organizing framework rather than a confirmed causal hypothesis'"
- **Abstract says:** "The evidence is therefore best treated as an organizing framework rather than a confirmed causal hypothesis."
- **Problem:** The authors describe the *evidence*, not "the field," this way. The quoted words are accurate but the frame around them is not.
- **Suggested fix:** "The authors conclude the evidence is 'best treated as an organizing framework rather than a confirmed causal hypothesis'."

**Issue C. Novelty label and preclinical detail** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research" / "specific mouse strains (BTBR, Ts65Dn) and valproate-exposed rats"
- **Abstract says:** "Preclinical data support biological plausibility—particularly for choline in BTBR, maternal immune-activation/CHRNA7, and Ts65Dn models and for resveratrol in valproate-exposed rodents."
- **Problem:** A purposive narrative review with no new data does not overturn prior research; and the abstract says "rodents," not rats, and includes a maternal immune-activation/CHRNA7 model the digest drops. Also worth naming first author Tariq A. Alalwan (University of Bahrain) alongside Perna.
- **Suggested fix:** Novelty: "Corrective synthesis"; "…specific rodent models (BTBR, maternal immune activation/CHRNA7, Ts65Dn) and valproate-exposed rodents." Add Alalwan to the call list.

NS fit 5/10 is appropriate.

### Study 6: An eight-week parent-led program keeps autistic teenagers' job skills from sliding over the summer
**PMID:** 42790248 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (one Moderate)

**Issue A. Headline asserts an effect the authors say the study cannot establish** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "An eight-week parent-led program keeps autistic teenagers' job skills from sliding over the summer"
- **Abstract says:** "Preliminary between-group estimates provide a signal of potential benefit for parent-reported vocational readiness but are not intended to establish programme effectiveness."
- **Problem:** "Keeps… from sliding" states effectiveness, and additionally implies the study measured skill decline over summer — it measured parent-rated readiness at baseline and post-intervention, with no demonstrated regression in the comparison group. The caveats and pitch body are appropriately hedged, but the headline is the part that gets pitched.
- **Suggested fix:** "A parent-led summer program shows an early signal for autistic teenagers' job-readiness skills" (or "…hints at holding the line over the summer").

**Issue B. Module-completion denominator** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "nearly 90% of intervention parents completed all modules"
- **Abstract says:** "Among intervention completers, 89.7% completed all eight modules."
- **Problem:** The 89.7% is of completers (29 of 32 allocated), not of all intervention parents — a small but standard adherence-reporting distinction.
- **Suggested fix:** "nearly 90% of the parents who completed the study finished all eight modules"

**Issue C. "Teenagers" undersells the age range** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "autistic teenagers' job skills" (headline); "Sixty-four Saudi parent–child dyads, with autistic adolescents and young adults aged 15–21"
- **Abstract says:** "autistic adolescents and young adults aged 15-21 years"
- **Problem:** The body is correct; the headline narrows the population to teenagers when roughly the upper third of the range is adults.
- **Suggested fix:** "autistic adolescents and young adults" in the headline.

NS fit 5/10 is defensible — it is randomized but small, parent-reported, waitlist-controlled and retrospectively registered, all of which the caveats name.

### Study 7: Caregivers of children with congenital CMV report *less* emotional strain when autism is in the picture — at school age
**PMID:** 42853118 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (one Moderate)

**Issue A. Different instruments for the two age bands is not flagged** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Caregivers of 181 children with congenital cytomegalovirus… completed quality-of-life questionnaires, split into toddlers (1 to under 4) and school-age children (4 to under 11)."
- **Abstract says:** "Outcomes among toddlers were assessed using the Infant Toddler Quality of Life Questionnaire and school-aged children using the Child Health Questionnaire."
- **Problem:** The entire hook is a reversal of direction between age groups — but the two groups were measured with *different instruments*, so part of the apparent flip could be measurement rather than adaptation. This is a key limitation for the story's central claim and is missing from both the body and the caveats.
- **Suggested fix:** Add to body: "…with toddlers assessed on the Infant Toddler Quality of Life Questionnaire and school-age children on the Child Health Questionnaire — different instruments, which complicates direct comparison." And add to Caveats: "the age-group reversal is measured with two different questionnaires."

**Issue B. Author's advocacy affiliation overlaps with the recruitment channel** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Megan Pesch at the University of Michigan, who works on both cCMV and developmental-behavioral pediatrics."
- **Abstract says:** "Pesch M(1)(2)(3)… (2)National CMV Foundation, Tampa, FL" and "Caregivers of children with cCMV recruited by social media and nonprofit channels."
- **Problem:** The first author is affiliated with the National CMV Foundation while the sample was recruited through nonprofit channels — relevant to the self-selection caveat the digest already raises, and worth disclosing to the writer.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call Megan Pesch at the University of Michigan — note she is also affiliated with the National CMV Foundation, one of the channels through which the sample was recruited."

*Otherwise accurate:* N = 181, the a priori block-wise regression finding that birth-severity markers dropped out after adjusting for current morbidity, the toddler pattern (autism and seizures → more negative emotional impact), the school-age reversal (seizure disorder and autism → less negative emotional impact), and the null family-cohesion result. The "adaptation" interpretation in Why it matters is appropriately hedged ("hints") and flagged in the pitch angle. NS fit 4/10 is well judged.
